title: Chapter XXVI

teacherSummary.text: In London, Jane calls on Caroline, who receives her coldly and visits late. Jane finally admits Caroline's insincerity. Wickham's attention shifts to Miss King, who has inherited money.

vocabulary.definition: Act of abandoning a person or cause to which one is bound by allegiance or duty, or to which one has attached himself
vocabulary.context: Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “defection”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Nothing, on the contrary, could be more natural; and while able to suppose that it cost him a few struggles to relinquish her, she was ready to allow it a wise and desirable measure for both, and could very sincerely wish him happy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “relinquish”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + quis (Latin quaerere, "to seek"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Her aunt assured her that she was; and Elizabeth having thanked her for the kindness of her hints, they parted; a wonderful instance of advice being given on such a point, without being resented.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “resent”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + sent (Latin sentire, "to feel"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Darcy’s sister, as, by Wickham’s account, she would make him abundantly regret what he had thrown away.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “abundantly”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from") + -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Do not involve yourself, or endeavour to involve him in an affection which the want of fortune would make so very imprudent.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “involve”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To sink or fall to the bottom
vocabulary.context: His apparent partiality had subsided, his attentions were over, he was the admirer of someone else.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “subside”: sub- (Latin sub, "under"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To strive, or to make efforts, with a twisting, or with contortions of the body
vocabulary.context: Nothing, on the contrary, could be more natural; and while able to suppose that it cost him a few struggles to relinquish her, she was ready to allow it a wise and desirable measure for both, and could very sincerely wish him happy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “struggle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To come back to, or come home to, as a matter of blame
vocabulary.context: “I did not think Caroline in spirits,” were her words, “but she was very glad to see me, and reproached me for giving her no notice of my coming to London.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reproach”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To give in return, whether good or evil
vocabulary.context: Her impatience for this second letter was as well rewarded as impatience generally is.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reward”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A man newly married, or just about to be married
vocabulary.context: The wedding took place; the bride and bridegroom set off for Kent from the church door, and everybody had as much to say or to hear on the subject as usual.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bridegroom”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Return visits were social signals; delay meant rejection.

significance: Wickham's quick switch to an heiress hints at his true motives.
discussionQuestions: What does Wickham's interest in Miss King suggest about him?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXVI,” how does Austen show cold reception? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXVI, how does Austen develop the idea of cold reception? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXVI develops the idea of cold reception. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of cold reception. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXVI suggests about cold reception. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXVI to complicate the reader's understanding of cold reception. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of cold reception responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of cold reception follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXVI and its treatment of cold reception. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXVI as evidence for a larger claim about cold reception in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of cold reception. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: To give in return, whether good or evil
To come back to, or come home to, as a matter of blame
A man newly married, or just about to be married

satQuestions.passage: “You are too sensible a girl, Lizzy, to fall in love merely because you are warned against it; and, therefore, I am not afraid of speaking openly. Seriously, I would have you be on your guard. Do not involve yourself, or endeavour to involve him in an affection which the want of fortune would make so very imprudent. I have nothing to say against him; he is a most interesting young man; and if he had the fortune he ought to have, I should think you could not do better. But as it is—you must not let your fancy run away with you. You have sense, and we all expect you to use it. Your father would depend on your resolution and good conduct, I am sure. You must not disappoint your father.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXVI”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Wickham's interest in Miss King suggest about him? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are defection, relinquish, resented, abundantly, involve. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do.” Webster's says: Act of abandoning a person or cause to which one is bound by allegiance or duty, or to which one has attached himself. Now the word history: “defection”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “relinquish”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + quis (Latin quaerere, "to seek"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “resent”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + sent (Latin sentire, "to feel"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Return visits were social signals; delay meant rejection. Why does this chapter matter? Wickham's quick switch to an heiress hints at his true motives. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to cold reception.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about cold reception, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
